lead: A parallel machine is only as fast as the paths between its processors. The interconnection network is the wiring and switches that carry data. Four classic shapes trade three costs: degree (links per node), diameter (longest shortest path) and bisection width (links cut when the machine splits in half). Mesh, tree, hypercube and butterfly pick different balances. Designers use them in supercomputers, multicore chips and network-on-chip fabrics.
prereq: You need Chapter 1.3 for separate processors joined by links, plus basic graph terms (node, edge, path).

blocks.text: A network has N nodes and some links. Four counts describe cost and speed.

items: Degree d: links at one node. High degree costs pins and router ports.
Diameter D: largest number of hops in the shortest path between any two nodes. A worst-case message needs D steps.
Bisection width B: fewest links cut to split nodes into two halves of N/2. A big exchange crosses this cut.
Link count: N × d ÷ 2 for a regular network, because each link has two ends.
Routing: rule for the next link; good networks keep it local and simple.

blocks.text: A k × k mesh puts nodes on a grid. Node (i, j) links to (i ± 1, j) and (i, j ± 1). An inside node has degree 4, an edge node 3, a corner 2. With N = k², links = 2k(k − 1), diameter = 2(k − 1), bisection = k. For an r × c rectangle, diameter = (r − 1) + (c − 1) and bisection = min(r, c).
A mesh is cheap: wires reach only neighbours. Its diameter grows as 2√N, so far corners talk slowly.

A binary tree gives each node one parent and up to two children. Internal nodes have degree 3, leaves 1, root 2. N nodes sit in log₂ N levels with N − 1 links. Diameter is about 2 log₂ N, leaf up to root and down.
Bisection width is 1: cut the link under the root and the tree splits. Every left-right message shares that link. A fat tree widens links near the root; data centres use this.
An n-cube has N = 2ⁿ nodes, each with an n-bit address. Two nodes link exactly when their addresses differ in one bit. The 3-cube has 8 nodes and 12 links.

Degree n, diameter n, links n·2ⁿ⁻¹ = nN/2, bisection N/2. It is recursive: two (n − 1)-cubes joined by 2ⁿ⁻¹ matching links. Routing: compare current and destination addresses, flip one differing bit; at most n hops.
Cost: degree n = log₂ N and a wide cut of N/2 links. Wires per node grow with the machine.

A butterfly is multistage: n + 1 stages, each with 2ⁿ nodes in a column. In stage i, node x links to the node differing in bit i in stage i + 1, and to matching nodes in stage i − 1. Interior switches have degree 4 (two backward, two forward); first and last stages have degree 2, so degree is at most 4. Any input reaches any output, and each stage settles one address bit. Butterflies realize permutations and serve the FFT and sorting networks. Price: many more nodes for fixed degree, easier to lay out than a hypercube's growing degree.

An embedding lays network A onto network B so B runs A's programs. Each A-link is simulated by a path in B. Dilation is the longest such path; expansion is B nodes per A node; congestion is the largest number of simulated links sharing one B-link.

Mesh into hypercube: for a k × k mesh take n = 2⌈log₂ k⌉. Use reflected Gray code: G(x) = x ⊕ (x >> 1), where ⊕ is bitwise XOR and >> shifts right. Give node (i, j) the address G(i) followed by G(j). Consecutive i or j values differ in exactly one bit, so each mesh link maps to one hypercube link: dilation 1. Expansion is 2ⁿ/k² ≤ 4.

Tree into hypercube: a complete binary tree with 2ⁿ − 1 nodes (n levels) embeds in the n-cube with small constant dilation and small constant congestion. A hypercube therefore simulates a tree with little slowdown.

items: Fully connected: degree N − 1, diameter 1. Fastest, impossible for large N.
Pyramid: degree 5 (four children plus a parent), or 9 if in-plane links exist at every level; diameter about log₂ N; mirrors quadtree image decomposition.
Perfect shuffle: degree 2 plus an exchange link, O(log N) diameter.
Cube-connected cycles: each cube node becomes a small cycle, degree 3, diameter a little over twice the cube's.

figure.caption: A 3-cube: eight nodes 000 to 111; every edge flips one bit. 000 → 001 → 011 → 111 takes three hops, the diameter.

spec.aria: A three-dimensional cube drawn as two squares joined by four matching edges; each node is a 3-bit address and each edge flips one bit.

examples.question: For N = 8 nodes, compare a 2 × 4 mesh, a balanced binary tree of 8 nodes, and a 3-cube. Give the degree, diameter and bisection width of each. Which network has the best diameter, and which has the worst bottleneck?
steps: Mesh: rows = 2, columns = 4. Diameter = (2 − 1) + (4 − 1) = 4 hops. Largest degree is 3: an inner node has two horizontal links and one vertical link. Bisection width = min(2, 4) = 2 links. The degree 4 in the table is for a square k × k mesh with k ≥ 3.

Tree: 8 nodes fill levels 0, 1, 2 and one node at level 3. Deepest node is 3 hops from the root; the deepest node on the other side is 2 hops away. Diameter = 5 hops. Internal nodes have degree 3. Cutting the one link under the root splits 4 nodes from 4, so bisection width = 1.
Cube: N = 2ⁿ = 8 gives n = 3. Degree = 3, diameter = 3 hops, bisection width = N/2 = 4 links.
Compare diameters: cube 3 < mesh 4 < tree 5. The cube is best.
Compare bisection widths: tree 1 < mesh 2 < cube 4. The tree is worst, because every left-to-right message crosses one link.
examples.answer: Best diameter is the 3-cube with 3 hops; worst bottleneck is the binary tree with bisection width 1 link.

traps: Bisection width is not degree. A 3-cube has bisection width 4, not 3.
The formula 2(k − 1) is only for a square k × k mesh. A rectangular r × c mesh has diameter (r − 1) + (c − 1).
An n-cube has N = 2ⁿ, so n = log₂ N. Writing N = n² or n = N/2 is wrong.
A binary tree internal node has degree 3: one parent and two children. Only the root has 2.
The butterfly is not a hypercube. It is multistage, degree at most 4, and uses many more nodes.

quiz.q: Define the degree and the diameter of an interconnection network.
quiz.a: Degree is the number of links at one node. Diameter is the largest number of hops in the shortest path between any two nodes.

quiz.q: For an n-dimensional hypercube, give the number of nodes, the degree, the diameter and the number of links.
quiz.a: Nodes N = 2ⁿ, degree n, diameter n hops, links n·2ⁿ⁻¹ = nN/2.

quiz.q: A binary tree has low degree and small diameter. Why is it still a poor choice for traffic between halves of the machine?
quiz.a: Its bisection width is 1. Cutting the one link under the root splits the nodes in half, so every message crossing the tree uses that single link and the root becomes a bottleneck. A fat tree widens links near the root to fix this.

quiz.q: A 4 × 4 mesh of 16 nodes is built. Find the degree, the diameter, the link count and the bisection width.
quiz.a: Degree 4. Diameter = (4 − 1) + (4 − 1) = 6 hops. Links = 2k(k − 1) = 2 × 4 × 3 = 24. Bisection width = k = 4 links.

quiz.q: A 6-cube is built. Find the number of nodes, the degree, the diameter, the link count and the bisection width.
quiz.a: N = 2⁶ = 64 nodes. Degree 6, diameter 6 hops. Links = 6 × 64 / 2 = 192. Bisection width = N/2 = 32 links.

quiz.q: Why does the butterfly keep a fixed degree while the hypercube's degree grows, and what price does it pay?
quiz.a: A butterfly switch uses at most 4 links in every dimension, so ports and wires stay constant. The price is size: n + 1 stages of 2ⁿ nodes each, far more nodes than the 2ⁿ of a hypercube, plus longer average paths and more hardware to clock.

quiz.q: You must embed a k × k mesh into a hypercube. Give the address mapping, the dilation and the expansion.
quiz.a: Use n = 2⌈log₂ k⌉. Address (i, j) as G(i) followed by G(j), where G(x) = x ⊕ (x >> 1). Consecutive i and j values differ in one bit, so a horizontal step changes one bit of the Gray-coded column field and a vertical step changes one bit of the row field. Dilation 1. Expansion 2ⁿ/k² ≤ 4.

beyond: Not for the exam. Chip makers sell network-on-chip fabrics where mesh and torus variants link 64 or more cores on one die, and data centres use fat trees and dragonfly graphs. Large Blue Gene supercomputers used a 3D torus. Engineers check bisection width, dilation and congestion before tape-out. Search next for network-on-chip topology, fat-tree data-centre networks and graph embedding dilation.
